docs.text: Hatchling ¶ This is the story of teaching a computer to play Snake. Not by writing rules for it, but by letting it play, fail and learn, millions of times over. A hatchling is a snake fresh out of the egg. It knows nothing about the world yet, and everything it does, it has to learn. That is exactly where this agent starts. How it started ¶ Snake is simple. You move a snake around a grid, eat food and grow. Hit a wall or your own body, and the game is over. The longer you survive, the harder it gets, because your own body fills the board. I wanted to see if an AI could learn to play it well. Not just chase food for a while, but fill the whole board. So I built everything from scratch: a game engine in C++, a terminal version you can play yourself on Linux or Windows, Python bindings so an agent could play millions of games, and the agent itself. The first agent was not very good. It scored around 55 points on average and kept running into its own body. Where it ended ¶ The final agent plays on a 20 by 15 board. It sees what a player sees, the board, the snake and the food, and it presses the arrow keys. It learns from the score and nothing else. It averages 267 points out of a possible 297. In about one game out of five, it fills every single cell of the board and wins. Nobody taught it how. docs.text: Contributing ¶ Contributions are welcome, whether it is a bug fix, a new experiment or a correction to these pages. Reporting a problem ¶ Open an issue with your operating system, how you ran the game or the script, and what happened. For agent problems, the output of play.py or diagnose.py helps a lot. Making a change ¶ Fork the repository. Create a branch for your change, for example git checkout -b feature/my-feature . Commit your changes with a clear message. Push the branch and open a pull request. Keep the engine independent of the game frontend and the Python code. It should only know the rules. If you change the rules or rewards in include/snake/engine.hpp , say so clearly in the pull request, because existing trained models were trained under the current values. Experiments ¶ If your change affects how the agent learns or plays, include a 200 game diagnostic of your model next to one of the released model. Results from single games are not enough to compare models. Experiments that did not work are welcome too. Some of the most useful parts of this project came from failed attempts, and Dead Ends is the place for them. Documentation ¶ These pages are built with MkDocs and the shadcn theme. To preview them locally, install the documentation dependencies and start the development server: pip install pip-tools pip-compile requirements-docs.in pip install -r requirements-docs.txt mkdocs serve The site is then available at http://127.0.0.1:8000 , and it reloads whenever you save a page.

docs.text: Diagnostics ¶ rl/diagnose.py plays many games with a trained model and reports how they ended. It is the most reliable way to compare two models, because single games vary a lot. Run it ¶ python rl/diagnose.py --weights snake_ppo_child_best.pt --episodes 200 The script plays 50 games at a time, so 200 games take about four minutes on a GPU. It reads the model's settings from the weights file. Option Default Meaning --weights The model to evaluate --episodes 100 Number of games --parallel 50 Games played at the same time --mask-reverse off Blocks the reverse key, fixed view only --merge-reverse off Treats the reverse key and the forward key as one move, fixed view only Reading the output ¶ This is the diagnostic of the final agent: Weights: snake_ppo_child_best.pt | View: fixed | Order: relative | Episodes: 200 | Time: 4.3 min | Mean score: 267.11 | Max: 297 Score distribution: min 1 | 10% 232 | 25% 282 | median 289 | 75% 294 | 90% 297 | max 297 Games ending below: <50: 4% | <100: 6% | <150: 8% Cause Count Share Mean score Forced Unforced wall 1 0% 1.00 0 1 body 157 78% 260.80 13 144 win 42 21% 297.00 Reverse key: pressed 813116 times (30.19% of moves), caused 37 of 158 crashes (23%) Body crashes by steps until the hit segment would have cleared (157 crashes): 1 (tail) steps: 8 (5%) 2 steps: 2 (1%) 3-5 steps: 4 (3%) 6-20 steps: 6 (4%) 21+ steps: 137 (87%) Scores The first lines show the average, the best game and the score distribution. The percentiles tell you more than the average alone. Here, 10 percent of games scored 232 or less, and half scored 289 or more. Causes Every game ends with a crash into a wall, a crash into the body, a timeout or a win. A crash is forced when all three moves were blocked, so there was nothing the agent could do. Unforced crashes had at least one free move left. Reverse key Only shown for the fixed view. It counts how often the agent pressed the direction it came from, and how many crashes followed such a press. Compare it with --merge-reverse before drawing conclusions, as described in Raising the Stakes . Crash distance For crashes into the body, how many steps the hit cell would have needed to clear. Crashes at 1 to 5 steps are usually timing mistakes near the tail. Crashes at 21 steps or more hit solid body, which on a nearly full board often means the snake had already trapped itself. Comparing models ¶ Run the same number of games for every model you compare. 200 games is a good default. With 50 games, differences of 10 to 20 points can still be chance.

docs.text: Setup ¶ This page sets up everything you need to watch the trained agent play, train your own agent or run the diagnostics. It takes a few minutes, plus the time to download PyTorch. Requirements ¶ Requirement Notes Python 3.10 or newer A C++ toolchain and CMake To build the snake_cpp module, see Building An NVIDIA GPU Recommended for training, not needed to watch the agent play A typical training run used about 2.7 GB of GPU memory and 1.2 GB of system memory. Watching it play or running the diagnostics also works on a CPU, just more slowly. Install ¶ Create a virtual environment and install the dependencies with pip-tools: python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install pip-tools pip-compile requirements.in pip install -r requirements.txt On Windows, activate the environment with .venv\Scripts\activate instead. PyTorch and the GPU ¶ The command above installs the default PyTorch build from PyPI. If you want to train on a GPU, make sure the installed build matches your CUDA driver. The PyTorch installation selector gives you the exact command for your system. Run it after the steps above to replace the default build. You can check that PyTorch sees your GPU with: python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available())" If it prints False , training still works, but it runs on the CPU and takes much longer. Build the engine module ¶ With the environment active, build the Python module: cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release cmake --build build --target snake_cpp Building it inside the activated environment makes sure CMake picks up the right Python version. Watch the agent play ¶ Download the trained weights, snake_ppo_child_best.pt , from Google Drive and put them in the repository folder. Then start a game: python rl/play.py --weights snake_ppo_child_best.pt --delay sets the pause between moves in seconds, so --delay 0.01 plays fast and --delay 0.1 lets you follow every move. The script reads the model's settings, such as its view, from the weights file, so no other options are needed. When a game ends, play.py explains the last move: Game Over (collision)! Final Score: 289 Moves: 16220 | Snake Length: 292 | Weights: snake_ppo_child_best.pt | View: fixed | Order: relative Last move options (snake length 292): Forward: body (265 steps from clearing) (chosen) | Left: 1 free cell | Right: 2 free cells Network input around head: Forward: body | Left: empty | Right: food Policy before last move: Up: 0.042 | Right: 0.903 | Down: 0.000 | Left: 0.055 | Value estimate: -17.48 Line Meaning Last move options What each move would have led to: free cells reachable, a wall, or body and how many steps until it clears Network input around head What the agent saw in the three cells around its head Policy before last move How likely the agent was to press each key Value estimate How good the agent thought its position was If the snake fills the board, play.py announces the win instead and shows the agent's last decision.

docs.text: Training ¶ Training runs rl/train.py . It uses PPO with 32 games in parallel and saves its progress as it goes, so long runs can be split into blocks and resumed. Train the final agent ¶ This is the setup of the final agent: the fixed view with arrow keys, and 8 of the 32 parallel games reserved for failure replay. python rl/train.py --tag child --view fixed --replay-envs 8 A run of 5 million steps takes a few hours on a mid-range GPU. The final agent trained for 30 million steps in six such blocks, each resumed from the end of the previous one: python rl/train.py --tag child --view fixed --replay-envs 8 --resume snake_ppo_child.pt --steps 5000000 The first 15 million steps used a death penalty of -10. For the last 15 million, DEATH_REWARD in include/snake/engine.hpp was set to -50 and the module rebuilt. See Rules and rewards . Resuming overwrites the best checkpoint A resumed run with the same tag starts its own record and overwrites snake_ppo_<tag>_best.pt at its first evaluation. Rename or copy your best file before resuming if you want to keep it. Files ¶ File Content snake_ppo_<tag>_best.pt The checkpoint with the best evaluation so far snake_ppo_<tag>.pt The final weights at the end of the run Every checkpoint stores the settings it was trained with, such as the view and the extra channels. The other scripts read them from the file, so you never have to pass them again. What the log shows ¶ Every 8,192 steps, training prints a line like this: Step: 4505600 | Avg Score: 129.47 | Entropy: 0.361 | Value Loss: 0.0579 | KL: 0.0012 | Clip: 0.010 | Replay Pool: 2417 | Replays: 7350 | Replay Share: 24.6% Column Meaning Avg Score Average score of recent normal training games. Training games pick moves with some randomness, so this is lower than the evaluation score Entropy How random the agent's choices still are Value Loss How far the value estimates are from the actual results. Sudden jumps can signal unstable training KL and Clip How much the policy changed in the last update Replay Pool Failure positions collected so far Replay Share Share of all training moves that came from failure replays Wins Training games that filled the whole board. Shown by the current version of the script Every 100,000 steps, an evaluation line follows. It plays 50 games without randomness: [Eval] Step: 4505600 | Greedy Mean: 188.90 | Max: 225 | Timeouts: 0/50 * The star marks a new best, which is saved as snake_ppo_<tag>_best.pt . Evaluation games are only for measurement and do not train the agent. Options ¶ Common Option Default Meaning --tag Name used in the checkpoint file names --view ego fixed for the board as a player sees it, ego for the snake centered view --steps 5000000 Total training steps of this run --resume Checkpoint to continue from --lr 0.00025 Learning rate. Resumed runs start at 0.0001 --gamma 0.998 Discount, how far ahead the agent looks --lam 0.97 GAE lambda --rollout 256 Moves per game before each update Failure replay Option Default Meaning --replay-envs 0 Parallel games reserved for failure replay --replay-horizon 200 Maximum moves per replay --replay-back-min 20 Earliest snapshot before a crash --replay-back-max 50 Latest snapshot before a crash --replay-pool 5000 Number of failure positions kept --replay 0.0 Chance that a normal game starts from a replay instead Endgame practice Option Default Meaning --endgame-envs 0 Parallel games that start from late game positions --endgame-length 250 Snake length from which positions are saved --endgame-every 25 Moves between saved positions --endgame-pool 2000 Number of late game positions kept This made the agent worse in testing. See Dead Ends before using it. Snake centered view Option Default Meaning --order relative Body order encoding, relative or inverse --head-channel off Adds a channel marking the head --tail-channel off Adds a channel marking the last 64 cells of the tail --danger-coef 0.0 Weight of the extra danger prediction task --long-start 0.0 Share of games that start with a long snake --long-min 100 Shortest snake for those games --long-max 250 Longest snake for those games These options only apply to the snake centered view and are not used by the final agent.

docs.text: Engine ¶ The engine is the heart of the project. It holds the complete state of a game and applies the rules, and it knows nothing about screens or neural networks. The terminal game and the Python environment are both thin layers on top of it. Moves and steps ¶ The engine thinks in relative moves: forward, left and right. Each call to step moves the snake once and returns a result with four fields. Field Meaning reward The reward for this move, see Rules and rewards done The game ended with a crash or a win truncated The game was cut off by the step limit score The number of food items eaten so far The board buffer ¶ The engine keeps the board as a stack of five grids of size 15 by 20. Each cell holds a value from 0 to 255. Channel Content 0 Head position 1 Neck position, the body cell right behind the head 2 All body cells 3 Body order, how soon each body cell will clear 4 Food position The body order channel can be encoded in two ways. In the default relative encoding, the value of a cell is proportional to the share of the snake that still has to pass before it clears. In the inverse encoding, cells near the tail get the highest values. The final agent does not use this channel at all. The buffer is exposed to Python without copying, so reading it on every step costs almost nothing. Useful extras ¶ Besides playing normally, the engine supports a few things that training relies on. Feature What it does Reset with a length Starts a game with a snake of any length, laid out randomly on the board Danger check Reports which of the three moves would end the game right away Tail segments Returns the last cells of the snake, starting from the tail Clone and restore Copies the complete game state and loads it back later Clone and restore are what make failure replay possible. A training game can save its state every few moves, and any saved state can later start a new game. The Python environment ¶ rl/env.py wraps the engine in a standard Gymnasium environment called SnakeEnv . It turns the board buffer into what the network sees, and it supports two views. Fixed view The view the final agent uses. The network sees the whole board with a one cell wall around it, so the input is 17 by 22 cells. It has six channels: head, neck, body, tail, food and wall. The agent chooses between four absolute moves: up, right, down and left. Pressing the direction the snake came from keeps it going straight. Snake centered view The view of the earlier agents. The board is rotated and shifted so that the head is always in the center, facing up, in a 39 by 39 window. It has four channels: body, body order, food and wall. Optional extra channels mark the head or the last 64 cells of the tail. The agent chooses between three relative moves: forward, left and right. The environment also exposes the engine's extras to the training code. reset accepts a starting length, danger returns the danger check, and snapshot and restore save and load complete game states.

docs.text: Playing ¶ You can play Hatchling yourself in a terminal. No setup is needed if you use a prebuilt binary. Download ¶ Every release comes with ready-to-run binaries for Linux and Windows. Download the one for your system and start it from a terminal. Linux chmod +x snake-linux-x86_64 ./snake-linux-x86_64 The Linux binary links the C++ runtime statically, so it runs on most distributions without extra packages. Windows .\snake-windows-x86_64.exe Run it from Command Prompt or PowerShell. Modern Windows terminals display the board correctly out of the box. If you prefer to compile it yourself, see Building . Controls ¶ Key Action W or Up Move up S or Down Move down A or Left Move left D or Right Move right Q or Esc Quit The snake cannot turn back into itself. If you press the direction you came from, it simply keeps going straight. The board ¶ The board is 20 cells wide and 15 cells tall. The snake starts with 3 cells in the middle of the board, moving right. +----------------------------------------+ | | | * | | o o o @ | | | +----------------------------------------+ Score: 0 The head is @ , the body is o and the food is * . Every food you eat adds one point to the score and one cell to the snake. The game ends when you hit a wall or your own body, and you win if the snake fills the whole board, which means a score of 297. The game advances every 100 milliseconds. You can change the speed and the board size in src/app/main.cpp before building it yourself.

docs.text: Rules and rewards ¶ The game follows classic Snake rules with a few details that matter for training. All of them are defined as constants in include/snake/engine.hpp . The rules ¶ The snake starts with 3 cells in the middle of a 20 by 15 board, moving right. On every step, it moves one cell forward. It can keep going straight or turn left or right, but never reverse into itself. When the head reaches the food, the snake grows by one cell and new food appears on a random empty cell. When the head hits a wall or any part of the body, the game ends. That includes the tail. The tail would move away on the same step, but the engine still counts it as body, so every piece of body is fatal. If the snake fills all 300 cells, the game is won. Rewards ¶ Every step returns a reward. These are the values the final agent was trained with: Event Reward Game ends Step into an empty cell -0.01 No Eat food +10 No Hit a wall or the body -50 Yes Fill the whole board +100 Yes The death penalty was -10 for most of the project. It was raised to -50 for the last part of training, which is described in Raising the Stakes . The step limit ¶ A snake that keeps moving without eating would never end the game, so there is a limit. If the snake makes 100 moves for every cell of its length without eating, the game is cut off. A snake of length 3 gets 300 moves, a snake of length 100 gets 10,000. A game that hits this limit is reported as truncated, not as a loss. It gets no penalty, and training treats it as an interrupted game rather than a failure. The constants ¶ Constant Final value Meaning STEP_REWARD -0.01 Reward for every move FOOD_REWARD 10.0 Reward for eating DEATH_REWARD -50.0 Reward for crashing DEATH_PER_LENGTH 0.0 Extra crash penalty per cell of length WIN_REWARD 100.0 Reward for filling the board MAX_STEPS_PER_LENGTH 100 Moves without food allowed per cell of length TAIL_IS_SOLID true Whether the tail blocks the head Changing any of them requires a rebuild . A model trained under one set of rules may play worse under another, so keep the values with the model if you share it.

docs.text: The Beginning ¶ Before an agent could learn anything, the game had to exist. I wrote it in C++17. The rules of Snake are small, but an agent needs millions of games to learn, and every microsecond per move adds up over that many games. The engine ¶ The most important decision was to keep the engine separate from everything else. The engine knows the rules: where the snake is, where the food is and what happens on each move. It knows nothing about screens, keyboards or neural networks. That separation paid off again and again, because the same engine runs both the terminal game and the training environment, and nothing had to be written twice. A game you can play ¶ On top of the engine sits a small terminal game for Linux and Windows. You steer with the arrow keys or WASD on a board 20 cells wide and 15 cells tall. +----------------------------------------+ | | | * | | | | o o o @ | | | +----------------------------------------+ Score: 0 The head is @ , the body is o and the food is * . That is the whole interface, and it is also exactly the picture the agent would one day learn from. The bridge to Python ¶ Neural networks live in Python, so the engine needed a way in. I used pybind11 to expose it as a Python module called snake_cpp , wrapped in a standard Gymnasium environment. Every move returns four things: the reward, whether the game is over, whether the step limit cut it off, and the score. The board comes out as a stack of grids, one per kind of thing on it. One grid marks the head, others mark the body, the food and so on. A neural network reads that directly, the way it reads the color channels of an image. The board is shared with Python without copying, so reading it costs almost nothing. Tools for later ¶ Two features did not matter on day one but became important later. The engine can start a game with a snake of any length, laid out randomly on the board, which makes it possible to practice crowded boards without playing a whole game first. Later, it also learned to save and restore its complete state. That one became the key to replaying the agent's own mistakes in Learning from Mistakes .

docs.text: First Steps ¶ The first agent used DQN, short for Deep Q-Network. It is one of the classic methods in reinforcement learning and a natural place to start. How it learns ¶ For every situation, the network guesses how good each possible move is. It picks the move it thinks is best, sees what actually happened and corrects its guess. The agent had three moves: go straight, turn left or turn right. It got a reward for eating, a penalty for dying and a tiny cost for every step. At the start it knows nothing, and its moves are random. Slowly the corrections pile up and patterns appear. Food is good. Walls are bad. The first bug ¶ The early results were strange. Games ended at odd moments, and learning was slower than it should have been. The cause was a bug in the step counter. The engine counts how many moves the snake makes without eating and ends the game if that goes on too long. That counter was not working as intended, and it was distorting how games ended. Once it was fixed, the agent started to improve properly. Seeing the board from the snake's eyes ¶ The biggest early jump did not come from the learning method. It came from how the agent saw the board. At first, the agent saw the board as a fixed map, like a player looking at the screen. Then I rotated and shifted the view so that the snake's head was always in the center, always facing up. From the snake's point of view, "left" now always meant the same thing, and a wall ahead always looked the same, no matter where on the board the snake was. At the same point in training, the score went from about 1 to about 7. That view stayed with the project for a long time. Much later, it would be questioned again. Where DQN ended ¶ After the fixes, the DQN agent averaged around 55 to 60 points. It learned to chase food and avoid walls, but it kept dying as it grew. A long snake fills the board with its own body, and the agent had no real plan for that. It would eat, grow and eventually trap itself.

docs.text: Looking Ahead ¶ To get past the DQN agent, I switched to PPO, short for Proximal Policy Optimization. Everything that follows in this story is built on it. A different way to learn ¶ Instead of scoring each move, PPO learns a policy directly: in this situation, how likely should each move be? A second output estimates how good the current position is, which is called the value. Training runs 32 games in parallel. The agent plays 256 moves in each, learns from all of them at once and then plays again. The first PPO agent averaged about 107 points, already a big step up from DQN. The discount ¶ Every reinforcement learning agent has a setting called the discount, usually written as gamma. It decides how much the agent cares about the future. A reward right now counts fully, a reward one move later counts a little less, and a reward a thousand moves later counts almost nothing. How far ahead an agent looks A discount of 0.995 means the agent mostly cares about the next 200 moves or so. With 0.998, that grows to roughly 500 moves. The first PPO agent used 0.995. That sounds close to 1, but for Snake it is short. A long snake can trap itself with a decision made long before the trap closes. I raised the discount to 0.998 and adjusted a related setting, lambda, to 0.97. The average jumped from 107 to 150.5. No new network and no new tricks, just an agent that cared about a longer future. It became the reference model for a long time, and I called it foresight. Variations ¶ Once foresight worked, I tried a few variations around it. Each one changed a single thing and was measured over 200 games. Experiment Average score Foresight (gamma 0.998) 150.5 Longer rollouts (512 moves) 137.9 Starting some games with a long snake 153.9 A bigger death penalty for longer snakes 157.4 Some helped a little and one made things worse. None came close to the jump from the discount. Measuring properly ¶ Around this time, I built a diagnostic tool. It plays 200 games and reports how each one ended: wall or body, and whether the crash was forced with every move blocked, or whether a free move was left. A single game can mislead you badly. Once, a new model lost its first two games at 38 and 56 points and looked worse than the old one. Over 200 games, it was the best model so far. From here on, every result in this story comes from a 200 game diagnostic, and the diagnostics were about to show something odd.

docs.text: Confident Blunders ¶ With the diagnostic tool in place, I could finally see how the agent died. Most deaths were crashes into the snake's own body, which was not surprising. How they happened was. Sure, and wrong ¶ The agent was not trapped. There was usually free space right next to it. And it was not unsure either, because it chose the fatal move with high confidence, often 60 to 100 percent. Its own value estimate did not see it coming. Right before crashing, it typically rated its position as good. About three out of four of these crashes hit a part of the body that was nowhere near clearing. It was solid body, in plain view, directly in front of the head. Asking the agent what it sees ¶ To find out why, I gave the network an extra task. Next to choosing a move, it had to predict which of its three moves would kill it right away. The engine knows the correct answer for every move, so this could be trained directly. The network got very good at it and caught 99.7 percent of fatal moves during training. And yet, in the games where it crashed, the prediction failed exactly on the fatal move. In this one, body was directly ahead, the agent was 95 percent sure about going forward, and it rated the chance of dying there at half a percent: Last move options: Forward: body (191 steps from clearing) (chosen) | Left: 63 free cells | Right: 4 free cells Policy before last move: Forward: 0.955 | Left: 0.045 | Right: 0.000 Predicted danger before last move: Forward: 0.005 | Left: 0.000 | Right: 0.079 The same shape, again and again ¶ When I put several of these crashes side by side, the same picture kept appearing. The head sat inside a straight line of its own body, with the neck directly behind it and another piece of body directly in front of it on the same line. In that one shape, the agent read the cell ahead as safe. It happened five times in a row in the games I watched. I marked the head explicitly in the input, so the network always knew where it was. The blunder stayed, and the danger prediction did not remove it either. Rare, not invisible ¶ So I ran a separate test outside of normal training. I collected hundreds of thousands of positions and trained a network only to spot fatal moves, with no rewards and no game. It learned almost perfectly and missed 6 fatal moves out of 85,018. When I showed it the straight line shape often enough, it got every case right. The network could see the danger. The problem was how rarely the shape appeared: Random play In 150,000 positions from random games with long snakes, the straight line shape appeared 39 times . The agent's own games In 200,000 positions from the agent's own games, it appeared about 7 times . A situation that almost never comes up in training never gets learned. Giving the agent more practice with exactly those situations is what Learning from Mistakes is about.

The problem was how rarely the shape appeared: Random play In 150,000 positions from random games with long snakes, the straight line shape appeared 39 times . The agent's own games In 200,000 positions from the agent's own games, it appeared about 7 times . A situation that almost never comes up in training never gets learned. Giving the agent more practice with exactly those situations is what Learning from Mistakes is about.
docs.title: Rare, not invisible

docs.text: Changing the Rules ¶ Over time, the game had picked up a special rule. The head was allowed to move into the cell where the tail currently was, because on the same move the tail moves away. Many Snake games work this way, and it sounds harmless. An exception nobody needed ¶ For a learning agent, it created a contradiction. Most of the time, body in front of the head means death. But if that piece of body happens to be the tail, it means nothing. The agent had to tell those two cases apart, and the only hint was a tiny difference in the input. I first suspected the agent had learned a shortcut from this. It often chased its own tail in a straight line, and in that situation the cell ahead was usually the tail. Maybe it had concluded that body straight ahead is often fine. That turned out not to explain the confident blunders , because the straight line blunder survived the rule change. But the exception was still a needless complication. A simpler rule ¶ I wrote the rule the way it should have been all along: Move into Reward An empty cell -0.01 Food +10 Anything else -10, and the game ends The tail is body, and body is fatal. I also removed the extra penalty for dying as a long snake, so every crash now costs the same. What happened ¶ I trained a new agent from scratch under the new rules. They are stricter, so it struggled briefly at first. Then it overtook every earlier model. The training average climbed to 130 to 138, against about 105 for foresight. In evaluation, the best checkpoint averaged 180 points, and the best single game reached 244. Something else disappeared too. Earlier models sometimes got stuck in endless loops at the start of a game. Under the new rules, those loops were gone in almost every evaluation.

docs.text: Learning from Mistakes ¶ The agent still made fatal mistakes in situations it rarely saw. Instead of changing the network again, I decided to show it those situations more often. Replaying the moment before a crash ¶ The idea is called failure replay. During training, every game keeps a snapshot of the board every few moves. When a game ends in a crash, the snapshot from 20 to 50 moves earlier goes into a pool. New training games can then start from one of those positions. The food appears in a new random place, so each replay plays out differently, and if the agent crashes again, that position goes back into the pool too. It works like a player who keeps retrying the part of a level that keeps killing them. A mistake in my own design ¶ The first version did almost nothing. After 1.6 million steps, only 75 games had started from the pool. The problem was how I measured it. I had set a quarter of new games to start from a replay, but the agent's games now lasted thousands of moves, so new games were rare. All replays together added up to less than one percent of the training moves. The fix was to reserve 8 of the 32 parallel games for replays. Each replay runs for at most 200 moves, and then the slot picks the next failure position. Now about a quarter of all training moves came from situations where the agent had once failed. The result ¶ Best earlier model With replay Average score about 151 178.5 Median score 179 212 Games below 100 28% 18% Best game 240 256 The earlier model is the last one measured over 200 games before the rule change. The replay agent continued from the model of Changing the Rules . The deaths changed character as well. A third of all games now ended at the wall, at an average score of 222, and most of those crashes were forced. The snake was boxed in on a nearly full board with nowhere left to go. That is a very different death from a careless blunder. Still a lot of help ¶ The agent was strong now, but it had a lot of help. It saw the board rotated around its head, it got an extra input showing the order of its body, and it had an extra network output trained to spot danger. I started to wonder whether all of that was actually helping.

docs.text: Like a Child ¶ By now the agent had a lot of help: a rotated view, a body order input and a danger detector. I started to ask a different question. What if I took all of it away? How a child learns Snake ¶ Picture a five year old with a Snake game. At first, they move around aimlessly. They hit a wall and the game ends, so they learn not to do that. They touch the food and the score goes up, so they learn to go for it. Much later, they start to plan and learn not to trap themselves. Nobody explains any of this to them. They see the screen, press the arrow keys and watch the score. So why was I giving my agent so much more? Taking the help away ¶ I built a new mode and called it child mode. In child mode, the agent gets only what a player gets. The screen No more rotating the board around the snake's head. The agent sees the fixed board with a wall around it, drawn as six simple layers: head, neck, body, tail, food and wall. Each cell is either one of those things or empty. The arrow keys Up, down, left and right, just like the terminal game. Pressing the direction you came from does nothing, also just like the game. The score The same rewards as before: food, death and a tiny cost per step. No body order input, no danger prediction and no rotated view. The only thing I kept was failure replay. A child remembers the spot where it died last time and tries again, so that felt fair. The neck and the tail get their own layers for a reason. A single still picture does not show which way the snake is moving or which end is the tail. With the neck visible, the direction follows from one frame, because the next cell continues the line from neck to head. With the tail visible, the agent knows which piece of body clears first. A child figures both out by watching the snake move, and the agent only ever gets one still picture. Slow, then steady ¶ Child mode learned more slowly, as expected, because it had to figure out everything the old setup had handed to it. I trained it in blocks of 5 million steps and resumed each time from where it stopped. Training Training average Best evaluation 5 million steps 67 73.5 10 million steps 139 188.9 15 million steps 148 210.1 At 15 million steps, the 200 game diagnostic gave an average of 192.8. That was better than every earlier model, including the one with all the help. A strategy nobody taught it ¶ Then I watched it play. The snake moved across the board in tidy columns: up, over, down, over, up again. It filled the board in a careful sweep, keeping the free space in one piece and avoiding little holes where food could get stuck. Nobody told it to do that. It only ever saw the screen, pressed the arrow keys and felt the score. The sweep was the strategy that kept it alive, so that is what it learned.

docs.text: Raising the Stakes ¶ Child mode played well, but late in the game it often died in situations that were not actually lost. The problem turned out to be in the rewards, not in the agent. Giving up too early ¶ In one game, the snake had 246 cells and turned into its own body. It could have gone into a free corridor instead, and as it moved through, its tail would have cleared a way out. The agent did not see that, and the rewards gave it little reason to look. Crashing right away cost -10. Surviving 18 more moves and then crashing cost a few hundredths in step costs plus a -10 that counts slightly less because it comes later. The difference was about 0.17 points. To the agent, staying alive a bit longer was worth almost nothing, so it rarely tried, and it rarely found out that some of those positions could be saved. Making death expensive ¶ I raised the death penalty from -10 to -50 and left food at +10 and the step cost at -0.01. The same comparison was now worth about 1.7 points, ten times more. I continued training the child mode agent with the new penalty for another 5 million steps. Afterwards, half of all games ended with the snake covering at least 87 percent of the board. Death penalty -10 Death penalty -50 Average score 192.8 224.9 Median score 220 262 Games below 100 15% 12% Best game 265 287 A button that did nothing ¶ Two games in a row ended the same way. The snake was moving down and the agent pressed Up. Pressing the reverse direction does nothing in Snake, so the snake kept going down, straight into its own body. The diagnostic made it look serious. The agent pressed the reverse key in 29 percent of its moves, and 58 percent of its crashes came right after a reverse key press. So I tested it in two ways. Normal play Average score 224.9 . The agent uses the reverse key as it learned to. Reverse key blocked Average score 203.9 . Without the key, the agent falls back to its second choice, which is often a turn it never meant to make. Reverse merged into forward Average score 225.2 . Forward and reverse do the same thing, so their probabilities are added together and treated as one move. Merging the two keys changed nothing. The agent simply used the reverse key as a normal "keep going" key, and those crashes would have happened with the forward key too. Meanwhile, the merged test had produced a game of 291, just six cells short of a full board.

docs.text: Dead Ends ¶ Not every idea worked, and some made things clearly worse. These are the experiments that did not make it into the final agent. Different ways to show the body ¶ The order of the body matters, because it tells you which parts clear first. I tried several ways to put that into the input. One version marked the cells closest to the tail most strongly. It reduced crashes right next to the tail but caused more crashes elsewhere, and the average fell to 132.4. A plain count of steps until each cell clears looked promising on paper. When I checked the actual values, it was almost identical to what the agent already had, so I dropped it before training. Marking the head and predicting danger ¶ When the confident blunders appeared, I marked the head as its own input layer, so the network would always know where it was. The blunders stayed exactly the same. An extra network output trained to predict fatal moves reached 99.7 percent accuracy, but it still missed the rare straight line shape, and the average stayed around 151. Practicing the endgame ¶ After the first wins , I tried to teach the agent that winning was possible. During training, I saved positions from late in every game, whether that game was later won or lost. Six of the parallel games started from those positions and played on until the end. From those positions, the agent won a lot, and training counted 4,918 wins. But everything else fell apart: Evaluation scores Before the endgame practice started, evaluations reached 190 to 230. Afterwards, they collapsed to mostly between 40 and 130. Early loops Loops at the start of the game came back. In some evaluations, up to 46 of 50 games timed out. Value estimates The value loss, usually between 0.1 and 0.5, jumped to between 1 and 5. Training became unstable. One network had to learn two very different worlds at once: games that end in a win after a few hundred moves, and games that take thousands of moves to get anywhere. It could not handle both. A model that wins more and plays worse ¶ The best checkpoint from that run was saved just before the endgame practice started, so it was the 30 million step model plus 400,000 normal steps. It actually won more often, 26.5 percent of games instead of 21. But 16 percent of its games ended in an early loop, with the snake circling near the start and never going for the food, and its average fell to 233. I kept the 30 million step version.

docs.text: Where It Stands ¶ The final agent is the child mode model after 30 million steps of training. It sees the board, presses the arrow keys and learns from the score, with failure replay and a death penalty of -50. The final model ¶ Average score 267.1 out of 297 Median score 289 Games won 21% Games below 100 6% Training 30 million steps The trained weights are available on Google Drive , so you can watch it play yourself. Most games end with the board almost completely full, and about one in five ends with every cell filled. What could come next ¶ The agent still loses most games in the last few percent of the board, usually because the free space has split into pockets it cannot fill. A few directions look promising. Starvation as a loss A snake that goes too long without food would lose, exactly like a crash. Right now, a game that hits the step limit simply ends without a penalty. Making it a loss would remove any incentive to circle forever and should end the early game loops for good. Gentler endgame practice The endgame practice in Dead Ends used six of 32 parallel games. Two would give the agent some practice at winning without destabilizing the rest of the game. Value estimates near the end The agent still expects to lose right before it wins. Any change that lets it experience more wins during normal training should help it recognize winnable positions and play toward them. The code, the trained weights and these notes are all open. If you take the hatchling further, I would love to see where it goes.
